## Incident Report: STRRAT RAT Infection — 2024-07-30

**Capture reviewed:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 frames, ~11.3 MB). No supplemental IDS/Suricata artifacts were present in the evidence directory — findings are derived entirely from the packet capture via tshark.

### Victim host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | `172.16.1.66` | Source of all outbound C2 traffic and DNS self-registration queries |
| MAC address | `00:1e:64:ec:f3:08` | ARP table (`arp.src.proto_ipv4`/`arp.src.hw_mac`) and consistent `eth.src` on all frames sourced from `172.16.1.66` |
| Windows hostname | `DESKTOP-SKBR25F` | NBNS name registration broadcasts from `172.16.1.66`; DNS self-registration (`DESKTOP-SKBR25F.wiresharkworkshop.online`); also embedded literally in the malware's own C2 beacon string |
| Logged-in domain user | `ccollier` | Kerberos `CNameString` in AS-REQ/TGS-REQ traffic from `172.16.1.66` to the domain controller `172.16.1.4` (`WIRESHARK-WS-DC`, domain `wiresharkworkshop.online`); also embedded in the malware's beacon string |

### Malware family

**STRRAT** (Java-based remote access trojan), reporting version **1.6**.

**Attribution confidence: signature-confirmed.** The malware's own C2 protocol names itself. Following TCP stream 83 (`172.16.1.66:49754 <-> 141.98.10.79:12132`) shows an unencrypted, pipe-delimited beacon repeating every ~5 seconds from first contact (frame 9066, t=76.99s) through the end of the capture (t=585.66s):

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender|UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy|1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

Field breakdown: literal string `STRRAT`; campaign/bot ID `1BE8292C`; victim hostname; victim username; OS `Microsoft Windows 11 Pro` 64-bit; installed AV `Windows Defender`; base64 field `UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy` decodes to `Program Manager` (active window title, a STRRAT info-gathering field); STRRAT version `1.6`; geolocation `US:United States`; and a running infection-uptime counter. This is the documented STRRAT ping-beacon format, sent in the clear over a raw TCP socket (no TLS handshake precedes it), which is itself consistent with STRRAT's known C2 behavior.

### Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint**
- `141.98.10.79:12132` — plaintext TCP beacon channel, ~2,100+ beacon exchanges (stream 83), confirmed via `follow,tcp,ascii,83`. No DNS lookup precedes this IP (hardcoded C2 in the sample) and no TLS/SNI wraps the session — matches the recipe's odd-high-port/no-TLS commodity-RAT C2 pattern.

**Domain**
- None captured for the C2 channel itself — the malware dials the C2 IP directly with no preceding DNS resolution for `141.98.10.79`.

**URL / delivery**
- No plaintext malicious URL could be extracted. In the ~13-second window immediately before the first STRRAT beacon (t=63.96s–67.97s), the host performed near-simultaneous DNS lookups for `github.com`, `objects.githubusercontent.com`, and `repo1.maven.org`, followed by an 8.8 MB TLS-encrypted download from `199.232.196.209` (`repo1.maven.org`, frames spanning t=68.0–73.8s, valid GitHub/GlobalSign certificates observed — legitimate infrastructure, not typosquatted). This is **behavioral, not signature-confirmed**: TLS content could not be inspected (no key log in evidence), so the payload/JAR/JRE bundle name and hash cannot be confirmed from this capture, but the timing is consistent with the STRRAT loader fetching a Java runtime/dependency bundle immediately before the RAT activated.

**File names / hashes**
- None recoverable. All payload-carrying traffic (the GitHub/Maven download and the C2 channel itself) is either TLS-encrypted or a raw non-file-transfer socket; no HTTP object export, SMB file transfer, or cleartext protocol in this capture carried the STRRAT binary. (HTTP export only yielded benign `connecttest.txt` from Microsoft NCSI and a geolocation JSON response — see below.)

**Supporting behavioral indicator**
- `172.16.1.66 → 208.95.112.1 (ip-api.com)`, `GET /json/`, User-Agent spoofed as `Chrome/73.0.3683.86` (frame 9111, t=77.87s) — a geolocation self-lookup occurring one second after the first STRRAT beacon, whose result (`US`, `United States`) matches the `US:United States` field embedded in every subsequent beacon. This ties the ip-api.com call to the STRRAT process rather than normal browser activity (no browser process traffic exists elsewhere in the capture).

### Benign context (ruled out)
Majority of traffic is legitimate Windows 11 / AD-domain-joined enterprise noise: Kerberos/LDAP/DCE-RPC/SMB2 to the domain controller (`172.16.1.4`, GPO retrieval), Microsoft telemetry/services (`*.msn.com`, `*.office.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, `events.data.microsoft.com`, `wns.windows.com`, Bing, Skype, NCSI connectivity check), Java auto-update check to `javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com`, and mDNS/LLMNR/SSDP/NBNS local discovery chatter.

### Incident summary
The Windows 11 workstation `DESKTOP-SKBR25F` (172.16.1.66, MAC 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08), logged in as domain user `ccollier` on `wiresharkworkshop.online`, was infected with the **STRRAT** Java RAT (v1.6, bot ID `1BE8292C`). Roughly one minute into the capture the host reached out to GitHub and Maven Central infrastructure over TLS, likely to stage a Java runtime/dependency for the loader, then immediately began an unencrypted C2 ping-beacon to **141.98.10.79:12132** that persisted for the remainder of the capture (~8.5 minutes, 500+ beacons), self-identifying the malware family, host, and user in every message.
